title: Government Transfers and Political Support
research_question: Do targeted government cash transfers to poor households causally increase political support for the incumbent government that implemented them, and do such effects persist after the transfers end? What mechanisms (e.g., voter learning about politicians' redistributive preferences versus reciprocity) account for any persistence of political support among former beneficiaries?
data_description: The analysis combines administrative records from Uruguay's Ministry of Social Development (MIDES) on PANES program applicants and beneficiaries with two purpose-designed household follow-up surveys collected in October 2006–March 2007 and February–March 2008, plus a 2005 baseline survey. The analysis sample contains roughly 1,942 households drawn from applicants whose predicted income score lay within two percentage points of the program eligibility cutoff (with eligible households oversampled 2:1). Key variables include an indicator for ever receiving PANES (administrative), self-reported support for the current versus previous government, confidence in the President and other institutions, household per-capita income, demographics, opinions about PANES and the successor Plan de Equidad, and various political/social attitudes. The unit of observation is the household. Latinobarómetro nationally representative surveys (2005–2007, ~1,200 Uruguayan households per year) are used to validate attitudinal measures and predict counterfactual support.
institutional_context: After a severe 2001–2002 economic crisis in Uruguay, the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition won the October 2004 election and took power in March 2005, ending decades of Colorado/National party rule. The new government quickly launched PANES (Plan de Atención Nacional a la Emergencia Social), the country's largest-ever anti-poverty program, running April 2005–December 2007. PANES provided a monthly cash transfer (UY$1,360, ~50% of beneficiary household income) and, for households with children or pregnant women, a food card, alongside smaller training, public-works, and health components. About 102,353 of 188,671 applicant households received benefits (~10% of all Uruguayan households). Eligibility was determined by a predicted income score based on baseline socioeconomic characteristics, with a sharp threshold; the scoring formula was developed by outside academics, kept confidential, and applied uniformly. In January 2008, PANES was replaced by the Plan de Equidad, which enrolled similar shares of former beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries near the original cutoff.
